problem: Existing VLN/VLA models (NaVid, NaVILA, UniNaVid) rely on dense large transformers plus ANN policies, causing high inference latency and energy that block on-board low-power deployment; efficiency work (COSMO, VL-Nav) remains dense and continuous.
motivation: Micro-robots, legged robots and deep-space robots need low-power real-time VLA. Event-driven SNNs only compute when information changes, so they could cut redundant computation across the whole VLA stack, not just one part.
key_idea: Convert every VLA component to spiking form: a differential-coding spiking SigLIPv2 encoder (Spike-V), a spiking multimodal LLM with channel-wise temporal sparsity (Spike-L), and a Laplacian-kernel population-coded spiking PPO locomotion policy (Spike-A).
insight: Spiking conversion of vision and language modules gives most of the energy saving (about 141 J -> 49 J) with a small accuracy loss (R2R-CE SR 53.9 -> 53.3), and it beats INT4-quantised NaVILA in accuracy at similar or lower energy (INT4 SR 48.2, 72.49 J). The time step T trades accuracy for energy (T=8 vs 16: SR 51.39 vs 53.29; Eng 44.23 vs 49.09 J). Laplacian kernel gives the best reward among the spiking kernels, though it is still below the ANN (26.72 vs 33.45). Energy is theoretical (45nm MAC/AC estimates), not measured on neuromorphic hardware.
method: Spike-V (SpikeSigLIP): SigLIPv2 ViT with differential spiking neurons; linear layers use time-step increments, and LayerNorm/GELU/Softmax/attention products are converted by differential graded units via ANN-to-SNN conversion, calibrated on ImageNet, with no retraining of those operators.
Unified tokens: history frames (196 tokens each), current frame and text are concatenated into one token sequence for the LLM.

Spike-L: LLaMA-8B fine-tuned on real video, simulated, auxiliary navigation and VQA data, then converted with leaky IF neurons; L fine steps merged into multi-level spike tokens; second-order optimization; quantisation-like variants (SpikeLLM, OmniQuant) are used.

Differential temporal sparsity allocation: informative channels get a long spiking horizon T', others a single step, with a per-token zero-point shift to handle negative activations, and modality-level channel sets.

Spike-A: learnable Laplacian-kernel population encoder, deterministic soft-reset IF spike encoding, fully connected SNN layers, firing-rate decoder to continuous velocity; trained by PPO with surrogate-gradient spatiotemporal backprop.
Energy evaluation: theoretical 45nm estimate (E_MAC=4.6pJ, E_AC=0.9pJ) with SOPs = firing rate × T × FLOPs, plus the ACE metric.

setting.backbone: SpikeSigLIP (SigLIPv2, ANN-to-SNN) + spiking LLaMA-8B (fine-tuned) + fully spiking MLP policy (PPO)
setting.training_data: NaVILA-style SFT on real video, simulated data, auxiliary navigation and VQA datasets; ImageNet calibration for the visual encoder; PPO in Isaac simulation for the low-level policy
setting.observation: monocular RGB (current + history frames) and language instruction; low-level policy uses proprioception, LiDAR/height scan
setting.action_space: language-level high-level actions plus low-level continuous velocity commands for the Unitree Go2 quadruped
setting.simulator: Habitat (VLN-CE R2R/RxR) and Isaac Sim (VLN-CE-Isaac, Unitree Go2)

numbers_note: Some tables contain empty rows (SpikeVLA-spikellm+encoder-snn, SpikeVLA-Vision). The split name for VLN-CE-Isaac is not stated and val-unseen is assumed. The first R2R table lists NaVILA NE 5.22 while the main table lists 5.28. The low-level control results (linear/angular velocity error) are not for a nav benchmark.
results: On R2R-CE val-unseen, SpikeVLA reaches SR 53.3 / SPL 47.9 against NaVILA's 53.9 / 49.3, using about 34% of the energy (49.09 J vs 141.25 J) and 6.2 GB vs 16.1 GB memory. On RxR-CE it gets SR 51.9 vs 52.3. It beats INT4 NaVILA (SR 48.2). On VLN-CE-Isaac it is slightly lower in SR (32.7 vs 36.5).
limitations: Energy is theoretical (45nm estimates) and measured only on GPU; no neuromorphic hardware or real robot validation.
Modest drop in SR/SPL versus NaVILA, and the SNN low-level policy is worse than the ANN in reward and linear velocity error (0.42 vs 0.23).
Paper is unfinished in places (empty table rows, duplicated tables, inconsistent numbers, inconsistent ablation labels), and the method descriptions are sparse.
